steps.label: the sentence the PR hangs on
steps.title: Why a HID package reaches for a video stream
steps.narration: UniversalConnection is thin. Connect, encode a payload, write it. That could have been the whole package. But the device refuses a touch report unless a media stream is running, so something has to own a video stream nobody wants video from. That something is Session, which is why 523 of the 1,754 lines sit in one file.

claims.text: nothing in UniversalConnection gates touch on a stream, the gate lives entirely in Session
claims.evidence: hid.go holds no stream reference, and ios/hid is the only importer of ios/display

steps.label: this one is invented, the others discovered
steps.title: Three constants, two kinds
steps.narration: 257 and 1281 already exist on the device and it enumerates them back to you, which is why the comment says to prefer what ListConnectedServices reports. SurfaceKeyboardDefault is different in kind. There is no keyboard until this package registers one, so that number is an invention of this code.

claims.text: SurfaceKeyboardDefault is invented here, while 257 and 1281 are enumerated by the device
claims.evidence: from the comment at hid.go:25-27, never observed against a device this session

steps.question: If the device assigns a different id than requested, is the returned value used everywhere?

steps.label: fire and forget ends here
steps.title: A nil error means written, not acted on
steps.narration: Nothing reads a reply. SendReport returns once the payload is encoded and written, so a nil error tells you the report left the host, not that anything happened on screen. This is the contract a caller is most likely to misread.

claims.text: SendReport returns once xpc has encoded and written, nothing reads a reply
claims.evidence: traced SendReport to conn.Send to EncodeMessage, ios/xpc/xpc.go:53-68

steps.label: registered, not discovered
steps.title: The rest of the connection, and the one asymmetry
steps.narration: Everything else here is a thin wrapper: build a payload, send it. CreateKeyboardService is the exception, because it is the only call that both sends and reads a reply, and the only one that brings a surface into existence rather than addressing one that is already there.

claims.text: the device echoes back the id it settled on and can omit it, in which case the requested one is used
claims.evidence: the fallback at hid.go:109

steps.label: the device rejects any other size
steps.title: report.go: the byte layouts, and why the sizes are fixed
steps.narration: Mechanical, but not arbitrary. Each surface accepts exactly one report length and rejects everything else, so these constants are a contract with the device rather than a convenience. Worth twenty seconds, not three minutes.

claims.text: the device rejects reports of any other size for these surfaces
claims.evidence: stated in the comment, not tested against a device this session

steps.label: monotonic, not wall clock
steps.title: The timestamp only has to keep going up
steps.narration: Six bytes on the wire, masked to 48 bits, anchored to a monotonic origin. The device reads monotonicity and the gaps between reports, never absolute time, which is why any monotonic source works and why a clock change cannot corrupt a gesture.

claims.text: only monotonicity and inter-report deltas are read from the timestamp
claims.evidence: the comment at report.go:44 and the use of time.Since

steps.label: the full held set, not a delta
steps.title: Three builders, one surprising contract
steps.narration: Digitizer and touchscreen reports are plain field packing. The keyboard one is the surprise: it carries every key currently held down rather than a change, so releasing one key means rebuilding the whole bitmap without it. Bit 4 of byte 1 is the letter a, which is why a single keypress looks like 0x10.

claims.text: the three builders match their documented layouts byte for byte
claims.evidence: 6 tests in report_test.go pin every field position

steps.label: built at init so the runs cannot drift
steps.title: keys.go: an ASCII lookup table
steps.narration: 138 lines of mapping and nothing to decide. The one choice worth noticing is that the letter and digit runs are generated in an init function rather than written out, so they cannot drift apart by a typo. Characters with no mapping return false rather than a wrong key.

claims.text: KeyForRune returns false for unmapped characters rather than guessing
claims.evidence: TestKeyForRune covers the mapped, shifted and unmapped cases

steps.label: declared a keyboard so iOS hides its own
steps.title: payload.go: the descriptor blob, and what it is for
steps.narration: This blob declares the virtual surface as a keyboard, which is what makes iOS hide its on-screen one. The reports actually sent do not match this layout, and the device tolerates that, so the descriptor's real job is identification rather than description.

claims.text: the reports sent do not match the descriptor layout and the device accepts them anyway
claims.evidence: stated in the comment, the divergence was observed in captures rather than reasoned from a spec

steps.label: widths differ by position
steps.title: Three payload builders, one strict decoder
steps.narration: Two of these are trivial. The keyboard registration is not: integer widths differ by position, and every leaf inside the storage block has to carry its own type or the device rejects the request. That strictness is the reason this function looks so fussy.

claims.text: the payload shapes match what the device accepts
claims.evidence: 4 tests in payload_test.go, including the integer widths and the device usage pairs

steps.label: a connection, a stream, a receiver, a goroutine
steps.title: Session: what it owns and what it remembers
steps.narration: Four moving parts and two pieces of memory. The interfaces above it exist so the gesture layer can be tested without a device. Hold one question while reading: who closes each of these, and in what order.

claims.text: streamLost is the only field written outside the mutex, so it is atomic
claims.evidence: written by the drain goroutine at session.go:460, read by every gesture

steps.label: one stream, started late, rebuilt if lost
steps.title: ensureStream: the decision the package exists for
steps.narration: One stream per session rather than one per gesture. A stream costs about a second to negotiate and churning them has been seen to wedge the device daemon. So it starts on the first gesture that needs one, and if the host stops receiving it the next gesture tears it down and builds a new one rather than sending reports into a stream that is no longer there.

claims.text: a lost stream is re-negotiated rather than reused
claims.evidence: the streamLost check at the top of ensureStream

claims.text: repeated churn wedges the device daemon
claims.evidence: never reproduced deliberately, because recovery is a device reboot

steps.question: What happens to a gesture that arrives while the rebuild is in flight?

steps.label: drain before negotiate, on purpose
steps.title: The ordering inside ensureStream
steps.narration: Draining starts before the stream is negotiated, because the device begins sending the moment it answers and an unread socket makes it throttle. Then a fixed 300ms wait, deliberately not tied to the caller's context, because giving up there would mean renegotiating next time and that churn is the thing being avoided.

claims.text: the surfaces cannot be polled for readiness, so the wait is fixed
claims.evidence: polled ListConnectedServices every 50ms for 500ms, no field ever appears

steps.label: close first, then wait
steps.title: teardownStream: the ordering that deadlocks if reversed
steps.narration: The receiver is closed before the drain goroutine is waited on. Reverse those two lines and it hangs forever, because closing the socket is the only thing that ends a blocked read. This is the kind of ordering that looks arbitrary until it is stated.

claims.text: closing the receiver is what unblocks the drain
claims.evidence: the comment and the ordering at session.go:461

steps.label: the connection that started it may be dead
steps.title: stopStream: why the stop needs a second connection
steps.narration: A negotiation that timed out closed its own connection, so the service that started the stream cannot always stop it. The first attempt goes out on the existing connection and, if it fails, a fresh one is dialled with the same session id. Without this a wedged daemon left the stream running, which is the state a reboot is needed to clear.

claims.text: a new connection can stop a stream started on another one
claims.evidence: ran it three times against an iPhone14,6: RTP packet count went to zero each time

steps.label: release where the finger is
steps.title: Tap, Drag and Stroke, and the bug in the middle of them
steps.narration: All three funnel into stroke. The release lands at the last point actually sent, not at the end of the path. The earlier version captured the endpoint up front, so a stroke failing at sample three still released at sample ten, which the device reads as a flick to somewhere the finger never travelled. On a VoiceOver screen that is a real navigation command.

claims.text: the release lands where the contact actually is
claims.evidence: TestStrokeReleasesWhereTheContactActuallyIs, and reintroducing the old code fails it with 900 instead of 20

steps.label: released between characters, on purpose
steps.title: Type: registering a keyboard the device believes in
steps.narration: The keyboard surface is created on first use, then every character is pressed and released. The release between characters is not politeness: without it repeated characters collapse into a single keypress, because the device holds a key until a report arrives without it.

claims.text: repeated characters collapse into one keypress without a release between them
claims.evidence: the comment at session.go:261 and the paired SendKeyboard calls

steps.label: a stray release cannot desynchronise anything
steps.title: The streaming API, and the contact ledger Close cleans up
steps.narration: TouchDown, TouchMove and TouchUp exist for live input where samples arrive one at a time. The device tracks position rather than transitions, so a move is another contact report. TouchUp is a no-op when nothing is down, and Close lifts a contact left behind by an interrupted stream, so a dropped connection cannot leave the device believing a finger is on the screen.

claims.text: a stray release sends nothing
claims.evidence: TestTouchUpWithNothingDownSendsNothing

claims.text: Close lifts a held contact before tearing the stream down
claims.evidence: TestCloseLiftsAContactLeftDown

steps.label: a stub makes ensureStream a no-op
steps.title: The tests: how the gesture layer became testable
steps.narration: This is the seam that makes the rest of the tests possible. A fake records what each gesture put on the wire, and a stub stream satisfies ensureStream so it returns without touching a device. Ten tests here, twenty seven across four files, and they are why five claims in this tour say tested rather than read.

claims.text: the gesture layer is covered without a device
claims.evidence: 10 tests in gesture_test.go, coverage 65.2 percent for the package

steps.label: byte for byte, every field position
steps.title: report_test.go: the layouts are pinned
steps.narration: Six tests that assert each builder produces the exact bytes documented in its comment. This is why the layout comments in report.go can be trusted: if someone shifts a field, these fail rather than the device silently rejecting a report.

claims.text: every field position in all three report layouts is asserted
claims.evidence: 6 tests, including the timestamp masking and the keyboard bitmap

steps.label: the decoder is strict, so the test is too
steps.title: payload_test.go: integer widths and type tags
steps.narration: Four tests round-tripping the payloads through a real plist encode. They exist because the device decoder is strict in ways that are invisible in Go: an integer of the wrong width or a leaf missing its type tag is rejected, and the error tells you nothing useful.

claims.text: the payload shapes survive a real encode and decode
claims.evidence: 4 tests including TestCreateKeyboardPayloadIntegerWidths

steps.label: the guards, without a device
steps.title: session_test.go: what a closed session refuses
steps.narration: Seven tests on the parts that need no fake: interpolation arithmetic, the context sleep, and what a closed or tunnel-less session refuses to do. Short, but they cover the paths a caller hits when something is already wrong.

claims.text: a closed session rejects every gesture rather than sending on a dead connection
claims.evidence: TestClosedSessionRejectsEverything
